title: Linear Search: Finding a Value in an Array
description: Walk an array slot by slot, stop at the first match, and report the slot number — or -1 when there is none.
congratsText: You can now write a search function that reports where a value sits, and say what -1 means.
objectives: Explain what searchScore is handed and what it sends back.
Predict the slot number a search reports for a given target.
Explain why not-found must report -1 and never 0.
Apply the same search shape to a different array.
recap: searchScore takes an array, its size, and a target, and returns a slot number.
The loop stops at the first match; a missing target costs a full pass.
0 is a real slot, so -1 is the only safe way to report not-found.
searchAge reuses the shape unchanged — only the array and name differ.

chunks.text: A linear search walks an array one slot at a time and compares each value to a target. searchScore(int arr[], int size, int target) takes the array, how many slots it has, and the value to look for.

check.question: What is the third thing searchScore is handed?
options: The value it is looking for
The slot number to start at

chunks.text: Inside the loop, if (arr[i] == target) return i; does the work. The moment a slot matches, the function hands back i — the slot number — and stops walking.

check.question: When a slot matches, what is sent back?
options: The value stored in that slot
The slot number that matched

chunks.text: Because it hands a number back, searchScore is declared int, not void. It answers a question instead of printing one.

check.question: Why is searchScore declared int and not void?
options: It prints the slot number to the screen
It sends a slot number back to main

quiz.question: What number does found hold after this runs?
options: 78, the value that was searched for
2, the slot number where 78 sits
3, counting the slots from 1 instead of 0
1, meaning the search worked

sections.title: Where the Target Sits Changes the Work

chunks.text: With scores[5] = {90, 85, 78, 92, 88}, searchScore(scores, 5, 90) matches on the very first slot. It checks one slot and hands back 0.

check.question: How many slots does the search for 90 check?
options: One, then it stops
All five, then it stops

chunks.text: searchScore(scores, 5, 88) has to check every slot, because 88 sits last. Same function, same array — only the target moved.

check.question: What did the search for 88 hand back?
options: 5, the number of slots
4, the last slot number

chunks.text: If the target is not in the array, no return i; ever runs. The loop simply ends, and the last line of the function runs instead: return -1;.

check.question: When does the return -1 line run?
options: Only after every slot failed to match
Right away, before the loop starts

quiz.question: Type the number found holds after this runs.

chunks.text: Slot numbers start at 0. In scores, slot 0 is a real slot holding the real score 90. So 0 is already taken as a meaning: "found, at the front".

check.question: Is 0 a real, usable slot number?
options: No, slot numbers begin at 1
Yes, it is the first slot

chunks.text: If the last line of the function were return 0; instead, then searching for 100 — a value that is not there — would hand back 0, which reads exactly like a hit at the front.

check.question: What breaks when not-found sends back 0?
options: A miss looks the same as a hit at slot 0
The loop stops before checking any slot

chunks.text: No slot is ever numbered -1. That is the whole reason it was chosen: it is a safe answer, one that can never be mistaken for a real slot.

check.question: Why is -1 safe as the not-found answer?
options: It is the smallest number a function can return
No real slot is ever numbered -1

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build the body of searchScore.

chunks.text: searchAge(int arr[], int size, int target) is the same shape pointed at a different array: ages[5] = {19, 22, 18, 21, 20}.

check.question: What is different between searchAge and searchScore?
options: The array it gets handed and its name
The way it reports a value it cannot find

chunks.text: searchAge(ages, 5, 21) hands back 3, because 21 sits in slot 3 of {19, 22, 18, 21, 20}.

check.question: Why does searchAge(ages, 5, 21) give 3?
options: 21 is the third value in the list
21 sits in slot 3, counting from 0

chunks.text: Loop, compare, hand back i, and return -1; at the end. That shape never changes — only the array and the function name do.

check.question: What has to change to search a different array?
options: The loop and the comparison logic
The array handed in, and the name

quiz.question: What two numbers print, and what do they mean?
options: 0 then -1: a hit in slot 0, then no match at all
19 then 25: each search echoes back the value handed to it
1 then 0: one search succeeded and the other one did not
0 then 0: slot 0 for the hit, and slot 0 for the miss too
